land.text: the King Country (Rohe Pōtae), Ngāti Maniapoto land 'from Kawhia Harbour and the town of Ōtorohanga in the north to the upper reaches of the Whanganui River in the south', 'from the Hauhungaroa and Rangitoto Ranges in the east to near the Tasman Sea in the west', behind the aukati, 'a line of pā alongside the Puniu River near Kihikihi': a 55 km circle at 175.1 E, 38.6 S (33 land cells, about 8,350 km2; its north edge, 38.105 S, stays south of the Pūniu at about 38.04 S) minus the Hamilton 50 km circle that stands for the Waikato lost in April 1864, so that no cell is both lost and gained

successors.note: The King Country 'was made accessible to Europeans' by 1883 (King Country page); the Waikato had been taken in 1863-1865. The Kīngitanga itself continues as a Māori institution (Tūheitia Paki, king since 21 August 2006) with no territory.

capitals.name: Ngāruawāhia
capitals.note: Site of the June 1858 coronation and Kīngitanga capital until it abandoned and then taken by Cameron's troops on 8 December 1863 (Invasion page). Coordinates approximate.

capitals.name: Itinerant, Maniapoto country (King Country); no fixed seat
capitals.note: Tāwhiao page: 'For the next twenty years Tāwhiao lived an itinerant lifestyle, travelling among his people in Taranaki and Maniapoto settlements'; infobox tenure as Ariki of Te Rohe Pōtae 5 April 1864 - 11 July 1881; he made peace with George Grey at Pirongia on 11 July 1881, riding in 'from the Tainui settlement at Hikurangi, modern-day Taumarunui'. The King Movement page likewise names no seat ('wandering through Maniapoto and Taranaki settlements'). No page names a residence for 1864-1883, so the dot is a stand-in at the middle of the King Country circle.

rulers.name: Pōtatau Te Wherowhero
rulers.note: Accepted the kingship in September 1857, crowned at Ngāruawāhia in June 1858, died 25 June 1860.

rulers.name: Tāwhiao
rulers.note: Reigned 1860-1894 (infobox; died 26 August 1894); cut here at the dossier's end in 1883.

correction.text: the Waikato: Pōtatau's proclamation 'Let Maungatautari be our boundary. Do not encroach on this side'; Ngāruawāhia, the coronation place, is 10 km north of Hamilton

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. The King Movement page gives the king's boundary in his own words ('Let Maungatautari be our boundary') and that the king envisaged ruling Māori customary land while the Governor ruled Crown-acquired land; it gives no area. A 50 km circle round Hamilton (about 5,000 km2) is the stand-in; the 486,500 ha later confiscated (Invasion of the Waikato page) is the same order of magnitude. The allegiance of Te Āti Awa and Ngā Ruanui pledged at Ngāruawāhia on 10 April 1860 is not territory. Why the King Country is not in this shape: the King Movement page says Pōtatau's role 'was strongly embraced only by Waikato Māori, with iwi of North Auckland and south of Waikato showing him scant recognition' (closely quoted), although a footnote on the same page lists 'Waikato, Maniapoto and Hauraki' as the 'first circle' of supporters (the Pukawa meeting of November 1856). The pages are not reconciled; Maniapoto land is drawn from the April 1864 retreat, the date the King Country page gives for the Kīngitanga going there, and Hauraki is not drawn at all.

correction.text: the King Country (Rohe Pōtae), Ngāti Maniapoto land 'from Kawhia Harbour and the town of Ōtorohanga in the north to the upper reaches of the Whanganui River in the south', 'from the Hauhungaroa and Rangitoto Ranges in the east to near the Tasman Sea in the west', behind the aukati, 'a line of pā alongside the Puniu River near Kihikihi': a 55 km circle at 175.1 E, 38.6 S (33 land cells, about 8,350 km2; its north edge, 38.105 S, stays south of the Pūniu at about 38.04 S) minus the Hamilton 50 km circle that stands for the Waikato lost in April 1864, so that no cell is both lost and gained

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: after Ōrākau (April 1864) the Kīngitanga 'retreated southwards from the Waikato' and was 'eventually being forced to flee to Maniapoto land, later called the King Country' (King Country page), closed to Europeans behind the aukati ('a line of pā alongside the Puniu River near Kihikihi'), 'under threat of death'. Corrected after review in two ways. (1) How the King Country enters: the first draft showed it in 1864 with no event, doubling the drawn area; it now comes in by the new gain of April 1864 (/ledger/5, counterpart nobody), and keyframe 0 stays the Waikato circle alone (see its note). (2) Its extent: the first draft's 70 km circle at 38.5 S reached 37.87 S, north of the Pūniu line, and so re-drew Te Awamutu and Ōrākau, which lie in the Waikato lost in April 1864 (/ledger/4). It is now a 55 km circle at 175.1 E, 38.6 S (33 land cells, about 8,350 km2, north edge 38.105 S) minus the Hamilton 50 km circle (the Waikato stand-in), leaving 31 land cells, about 7,840 km2. The Hamilton stand-in reaches 38.24 S, so the two cells (about 506 km2) round Ōtorohanga, which the King Country page names as the northern edge of the King Country, fall under both circles and are left to the Waikato side. The circle is a stand-in (gazetteer_names_needed: King Country / Rohe Pōtae). No page gives an area.

region.text: the Waikato: Pōtatau's proclamation 'Let Maungatautari be our boundary. Do not encroach on this side'; Ngāruawāhia, the coronation place, is 10 km north of Hamilton

ledger.note: 1858: Pōtatau Te Wherowhero is crowned the first Māori king at Ngāruawāhia. The page: Wiremu Tāmihana circulated the proposal in February 1857, Te Wherowhero accepted the kingship in September 1857 and was crowned at Ngāruawāhia in June 1858 (closely paraphrased). The Waikato territory is the researcher's reading of the king's proclaimed boundary at Maungatautari.

region.text: the Waikato: Pōtatau's proclamation 'Let Maungatautari be our boundary. Do not encroach on this side'; Ngāruawāhia, the coronation place, is 10 km north of Hamilton

ledger.note: 1863: the invasion of the Waikato begins. On 9 July 1863 Governor Grey issued an ultimatum to swear allegiance or be expelled south of the Waikato River; on 12 July 1863 Cameron and the first echelon of the invading army crossed the Mangatāwhiri Stream near Pokeno (Invasion page, closely paraphrased).

1863: Ngāruawāhia falls. the Kīngitanga capital at Ngāruawāhia was abandoned and then taken by Cameron's troops on 8 December 1863 (closely paraphrased), after Rangiriri on 20-21 November; the king's seat then moves south into Maniapoto country (destination not named by the pages).

region.text: the Waikato: Pōtatau's proclamation 'Let Maungatautari be our boundary. Do not encroach on this side'; Ngāruawāhia, the coronation place, is 10 km north of Hamilton

ledger.note: 1864: the Waikato campaign ends at Ōrākau. Ōrākau was besieged from 31 March and the garrison broke out on 2 April 1864; 'The campaign ended with the retreat of the Kingitanga Māori into the rugged interior of the North Island.'

region.text: the Waikato: Pōtatau's proclamation 'Let Maungatautari be our boundary. Do not encroach on this side'; Ngāruawāhia, the coronation place, is 10 km north of Hamilton

ledger.note: 1864: the Waikato is lost; the Kīngitanga withdraws to the King Country. The Waikato was then confiscated under the New Zealand Settlements Act (passed December 1863; proclamations 30 January and 16 May 1865): about 486,500 ha, 'more than 480,000 hectares' (the introduction of the page says about 12,000 km2 and the figures are not reconciled). The date is the retreat, the page-dated end of the war.

ledger.note: 1864: the Kīngitanga withdraws into the King Country. 'the Kingite forces retreated southwards from the Waikato after the battle at Ōrākau in April 1864', 'eventually being forced to flee to Maniapoto land, later called the King Country' (King Country page). The year and the retreat are the page's; the land is the researcher's stand-in, and counterpart nobody is the reading that no state held Maniapoto land (the page: 'by 1883 the King Country was made accessible to Europeans'). The Tāwhiao page gives his tenure as Ariki of Te Rohe Pōtae as 5 April 1864 - 11 July 1881.

ledger.note: 1883: the King Country is opened. 'by 1883 the King Country was made accessible to Europeans'; in March 1883 John Bryce secured a compact allowing the railway to be surveyed and in February 1885 Ballance's meeting at Kihikihi approved construction. Tāwhiao had laid down the movement's arms in 1881 and gone to London in 1884.

wars.name: Invasion of the Waikato
wars.outcome: British victory: 12 July 1863 crossing of the Mangatāwhiri, Rangiriri 20-21 November 1863, Ngāruawāhia taken 8 December 1863, Te Awamutu 21 February 1864, Ōrākau 31 March-2 April 1864; the Kīngitanga retreated to the King Country and about 486,500 ha of Waikato were confiscated in 1865.
wars.note: About 14,000 British and colonial troops at peak against about 4,000 Māori warriors from more than half the major North Island tribal groups. Infobox dates: 12 July 1863 to April 1864.

certainty.note: A king's proclaimed boundary (Maungatautari), not a surveyed line.

The aukati, a line of pā on the Pūniu River near Kihikihi, was a recognised frontier closed to Europeans 'under threat of death'; the southern and eastern edges (upper Whanganui, Hauhungaroa and Rangitoto Ranges) are approximate.

sources.title: Tāwhiao
sources.note: Tried for the king's seat 1864-1883: itinerant for twenty years in Taranaki and Maniapoto settlements; Ariki of Te Rohe Pōtae 5 April 1864 - 11 July 1881; peace with Grey at Pirongia 11 July 1881; Hikurangi (Taumarunui); Kauhanganui at Maungakawa 1892. No fixed seat named.

notes: A state Cliopatria lacks; drawn as a king's land (a chiefs' federation under one king), not a sovereign state in the European sense: the Colony treated it as a rebellion. The King Movement's other claims (the allegiance of Taranaki iwi from 10 April 1860, the 1860-1861 Taranaki war, Tūhoe and Ngāti Tūwharetoa) are not territory on the pages opened. The 'Rohe Pōtae' name does not appear on the Invasion or King Movement pages (the King Country page uses it only through Tāwhiao's hat on the map). Not on any page opened: the king's residence 1864-1883 (Te Kopua is not mentioned), the Native Land Court, the date the aukati closed (1883 is 'accessible', February 1885 the railway approval), Tāwhiao's 1881 meeting beyond the King Movement page's account. The Kīngitanga continues to the present as a Māori institution (Kauhanganui 1892; Tūrangawaewae); this dossier draws only the territory. The counterpart slug 'colony-of-new-zealand' needs a dossier: counterparts_needing_dossiers. Region names: the Hamilton radius is the Waikato stand-in; the King Country is a coordinate stand-in, a 55 km circle at 175.1 E, 38.6 S minus the Hamilton circle (gazetteer_names_needed: King Country). Ngāruawāhia coordinates approximate. Review repair of 2026-10-18: (1) the King Country now enters by a gain of April 1864 (counterpart nobody, King Country page) and not in 1858; the choice rests on the King Movement page saying that iwi south of Waikato gave Pōtatau 'scant recognition', against its own footnote naming Maniapoto in the 'first circle' (pages disagree, not reconciled); the reviewer's alternative, adding the King Country to the 1858 found region, would draw Maniapoto land from 1858. (2) The circle is moved south and shrunk (55 km at 38.6 S) and the Hamilton circle subtracted, so it no longer re-draws Te Awamutu and Ōrākau; two cells round Ōtorohanga stay in the Waikato circle. (3) The king's seat 1864-1883: the Tāwhiao page was opened and names none (itinerant for twenty years), so the capital entry now says so.
